paragraphs: Vision and touch provide different kinds of evidence about an object's shape. An image supplies broad context, while contact reveals detailed information about a small part of the surface. This paper studies how to combine those signals for three-dimensional reconstruction, using a chart-based representation that organizes surface information into patches.

The researchers introduce a dataset containing simulated visual and touch signals from a robotic hand interacting with many three-dimensional objects. This provides a setting for testing whether the two senses help each other and whether the proposed representation makes their combination more effective. In these experiments, combining vision and touch consistently improves on using either modality alone.

The chart-based method also outperforms alternative ways of combining the modalities, and the results attribute substantial benefit to its surface structure. Reconstruction improves as more grasps become available. Touch also helps reconstruct the neighborhood around a contact point, suggesting that a local measurement can inform a broader surface region rather than correcting only the exact location touched.
neurips-2020-3d-shape-reconstruction-fro.tldr: A chart-based reconstruction method combines vision and simulated touch to improve object shapes, including surface regions near contact points.

paragraphs: Transformer language models can perform well across language tasks, but their initial unsupervised training requires substantial computation. This paper targets that training stage with progressive layer dropping. The central idea is to change how the network's layers participate in training so that learning requires less work, using architectural and training choices to improve efficiency.

The approach matters because accelerating training through additional hardware can make large models difficult to access. Here, the reported savings come from the training method itself. Experiments with BERT show a 25% reduction in floating-point computation and a 24% reduction in total training time. Reporting both measures establishes that the computational reduction also translates into elapsed-time savings in those experiments.

The authors also evaluate whether the resulting pretrained models remain useful for subsequent tasks. Their models achieve similar or sometimes higher downstream accuracy than the baseline models. These findings indicate that the tested reduction in pretraining cost can coexist with strong transfer to other tasks, rather than merely producing a cheaper model whose learned knowledge is less useful.
neurips-2020-accelerating-training-of-tr.tldr: Progressive layer dropping reduces BERT pretraining computation and elapsed time while preserving or improving accuracy on the downstream tasks tested.

paragraphs: Experience replay lets a reinforcement learning agent learn again from previously observed transitions. Prioritized Experience Replay changes how often transitions are selected, favoring those with larger temporal-difference errors. This paper examines the relationship between that sampling choice and the loss function used to learn from the selected data.

The main result shows that a loss evaluated under nonuniform sampling can be transformed into a different loss under uniform sampling with the same expected gradient. In other words, changing which examples appear more often can be represented through a change in the learning objective's gradient contributions. The equivalence concerns the average update, so it does not itself assert that individual sampled updates are identical.

In some tested environments, the transformed loss replaces prioritized replay without changing empirical performance. The authors also use the equivalence to identify improvements by correcting the uniformly sampled loss associated with prioritized replay. Experiments in several MuJoCo and Atari environments support those modifications. The contribution therefore provides both an explanation of replay prioritization and a route to improving it through loss design.
neurips-2020-an-equivalence-between-loss.tldr: Nonuniform replay sampling can be translated into a uniformly sampled loss with the same expected gradient, enabling alternative and improved replay methods.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks often learn by passing information between neighboring nodes. This supports learning local patterns while respecting changes in node ordering, but conventional message passing can miss basic properties of graph topology. The paper proposes structural message passing to make local representations more informative about how a graph is connected.

Alongside ordinary node features, the method propagates one-hot node encodings to construct a local context matrix around each node. These matrices contain information about both features and connectivity and can be pooled into node representations. The message and update functions are designed to preserve permutation equivariance: changing node labels changes the corresponding organization of outputs without changing the underlying graph information represented.

This design allows the model to use identifying encodings without making its conclusions depend on their arbitrary assignment. The authors connect that independence to inductive reasoning and better generalization. Experiments show more accurate predictions of several topological properties on synthetic graphs than previous methods, together with reported state-of-the-art molecular graph regression results on ZINC.
neurips-2020-building-powerful-and-equiv.tldr: Structural message passing enriches graph representations with local topology while preserving independence from arbitrary node labeling.

paragraphs: Multiple agents can share one policy network while choosing actions from their own information. This makes training efficient, but raises a question: what kind of equilibrium does shared training produce when agents have different types and only partial observations? The paper studies this setting in games where agents' interests need not be identical or directly opposed.

The authors define a Shared equilibrium through a symmetric pure Nash equilibrium in a related Functional Form Game. They prove that self-play converges to this equilibrium for a certain class of games. This gives a formal interpretation of shared-policy behavior while keeping the convergence claim tied to the class for which it is established.

The paper also introduces a dual reinforcement learning approach for matching emergent equilibrium behavior to externally specified targets. It calibrates parameters of agent-type distributions, allowing agents to behave differently while retaining a shared network that scales across agents. An example involving a market with multiple participants illustrates how this calibration can connect the behavior of a trained system to real-world modeling targets.
neurips-2020-calibration-of-shared-equil.tldr: The paper formalizes equilibria for agents sharing a policy and calibrates their collective behavior by adjusting distributions of agent types.

paragraphs: Pruning removes neural network weights to obtain a sparse model. This paper starts from the observation that stochastic gradient descent often reaches a broad, flat valley of training loss. Its directional pruning method searches for a sparse solution within or near that valley, aiming to remove weights through changes that have little effect on the training objective.

Directly identifying flat directions would be computationally difficult. The authors instead use a carefully tuned proximal gradient algorithm with an l1 penalty. They prove that it achieves directional pruning with a small learning rate after sufficient training. The proposed method does not require retraining or expert selection of the sparsity level.

Experiments with ResNet50 on ImageNet report promising performance at 92% sparsity, with only slightly greater time and memory costs than stochastic gradient descent. Additional experiments with VGG16 and wide ResNet on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 find solutions in the same loss valley as stochastic gradient descent. Their differences avoid directions that affect training loss, supporting the geometric motivation for the method.
neurips-2020-directional-pruning-of-deep.tldr: Directional pruning seeks sparse networks along flat training-loss directions, with conditional guarantees and promising results at high sparsity.

paragraphs: A learned dynamics model can be uncertain because it lacks knowledge or because outcomes contain inherent randomness. These are epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty, respectively. The paper argues that many model-based reinforcement learning methods distinguish them during model learning but fail to exploit the distinction when choosing actions, leading to insufficient exploration.

H-UCRL makes optimistic exploration practical by reparameterizing plausible dynamics models and adding imagined control inputs that act on epistemic uncertainty. These extra inputs let planning consider favorable possibilities within what the model does not yet know. By augmenting the input space this way, the method can use standard greedy planners to solve the resulting optimistic planning problem.

The analysis gives a general regret bound for well-calibrated models and proves sublinear regret for Gaussian Process models. The authors also combine the approach with different probabilistic models and existing reinforcement learning algorithms. Experiments show substantially faster learning when actions incur penalties. In that setting, optimism helps exploration despite the immediate cost of taking actions, addressing a reported weakness of existing model-based methods.
neurips-2020-efficient-model-based-reinf.tldr: H-UCRL turns uncertainty about dynamics into optimistic planning inputs, enabling practical exploration and faster learning in experiments with action penalties.

paragraphs: GradAug addresses overfitting by changing the training signals received by a neural network. During training, it samples subnetworks with different widths and regularizes them using randomly transformed training examples. Because these subnetworks come from the original network, their learning signals introduce disturbances into its gradients that are guided by related learning problems.

The intended effect is to encourage representations that are more diverse and generalize better. The authors describe the method as easy to implement and applicable across network structures and applications. For ResNet-50 on ImageNet, they report 78.79% classification accuracy, presented as a new state-of-the-art result. Combining GradAug with CutMix raises the reported accuracy to 79.67%, exceeding an ensemble of advanced training techniques.

The evaluation extends beyond image classification to object detection and instance segmentation on COCO, where GradAug substantially outperforms the compared methods. The authors also report robustness to image distortions and FGSM adversarial attacks, along with effectiveness when training data are scarce. Together, these experiments support the claim that the gradient regularization improves several aspects of representation quality in the tested settings.
neurips-2020-gradaug-a-new-regularizatio.tldr: GradAug trains width-sampled subnetworks on transformed examples to regularize gradients and improve generalization across the evaluated vision tasks.

paragraphs: A graph can contain useful patterns at several scales, from individual neighborhoods to larger structures. Graph Cross Networks, or GXN, learn representations at multiple scales and exchange intermediate features between them. This exchange lets information developed at one resolution contribute to learning at another while the network is still building its representations.

The first component, vertex infomax pooling, learns which vertices to retain when constructing smaller graphs. It uses a neural estimate of mutual information between a vertex's features and its neighborhood's features. The guiding idea is to retain vertices that reflect their surroundings well. A feature-crossing layer then combines intermediate features between two scales to enrich both representations.

The experiments report average classification accuracy improvements of 2.12% for whole graphs and 1.15% for individual vertices. With the surrounding network held the same, the proposed pooling method also consistently outperforms other graph-pooling methods. These results support both parts of the design: selecting informative vertices to construct multiple scales and allowing those scales to exchange information throughout feature learning.
neurips-2020-graph-cross-networks-with-v.tldr: GXN combines informative vertex selection with feature exchange across graph scales to improve graph and vertex classification.

paragraphs: Large convolutional networks can improve accuracy, but training them on resource-constrained edge devices is expensive. FedGKT changes how federated training distributes this work. Small networks train on edge devices, while a large network resides on the server, allowing the system to pursue the benefits of a larger model with less demanding local computation.

The method uses a variant of alternating minimization and periodically transfers knowledge from the small networks to the server network through knowledge distillation. The framework also supports asynchronous training and reduces communication bandwidth for large convolutional models. This organization makes the size of the server model less directly determine the training burden placed on each edge device.

Experiments use networks based on ResNet-56 and ResNet-110 with CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CINIC-10, and non-IID variants. FedGKT achieves comparable or slightly higher accuracy than FedAvg in these tests. Relative to edge training with FedAvg, it uses 9 to 17 times less edge computation and 54 to 105 times fewer edge-model parameters, demonstrating substantial local resource savings in the evaluated configurations.
neurips-2020-group-knowledge-transfer-fe.tldr: FedGKT transfers knowledge from small edge networks to a large server network, substantially reducing edge training costs while maintaining competitive accuracy.

paragraphs: Differentially private estimation problems can vary in difficulty from one dataset to another. A worst-case guarantee describes the hardest instances, but may poorly reflect what is achievable on a well-behaved dataset. This paper develops algorithms intended to approach the best attainable performance for individual instances by extending and approximating the inverse sensitivity mechanism.

The authors introduce two approximation frameworks. One needs knowledge only of local sensitivities, which describe how an answer changes near the given dataset. The other uses gradients for optimization problems. Both frameworks are efficiently computable for broad classes of functions. Instance-specific lower bounds for vector-valued functions provide a way to assess how close the algorithms come to the best possible performance.

Under certain assumptions, the mechanisms are nearly instance-optimal and can substantially outperform worst-case minimax benchmarks on favorable instances. The framework produces private methods for mean estimation with unbounded range, principal component analysis, and linear regression. For principal component analysis, it yields an efficient algorithm satisfying pure differential privacy with near-optimal rates, connecting the instance-sensitive theory to a concrete estimation task.
neurips-2020-instance-optimality-in-diff.tldr: Approximate inverse sensitivity mechanisms adapt private estimation to individual datasets and achieve near-instance-optimal performance under stated assumptions.

paragraphs: Feature attribution explains a prediction by assigning contributions to its input features. Those assignments can still be difficult to interpret: a model may rely on noise, and the attribution values alone do not explain why particular features deserve importance. This paper asks how additional information about features can guide both model learning and its explanations.

The deep attribution prior framework, DAPr, jointly learns a relationship between that prior information and feature importance. It also biases the predictive model toward explanations that emphasize features expected to matter. Rather than treating the extra information as a fixed list of importance scores, the framework learns how it relates to importance while training the model.

This creates a connection between the features used for prediction and the outside knowledge that makes their relevance interpretable. The authors find that the resulting networks generalize better to data outside the training sample and support new ways of interpreting model behavior. The approach is motivated by settings where additional feature information is available and predictive of relevance to the task.
neurips-2020-learning-deep-attribution-p.tldr: DAPr learns how prior feature information predicts importance and uses that relationship to guide explanations and improve generalization.

paragraphs: Sparse coding learns features whose representations use relatively few active coefficients. In neuroscience models, it offers an account of how neural systems might encode information. However, many methods overlook communication bottlenecks between brain areas. Compression can address these bottlenecks, but a dense random projection assumes widespread connections that conflict with observed local wiring.

This paper uses structured random matrices to model compressed communication while respecting local connection patterns. It asks whether unsupervised sparse representations can still be learned when the compression process has substantial wiring constraints. Both analysis and experiments examine several forms of compression matrix corresponding to different local wiring arrangements.

The authors find that sparse learning remains effective in the compressed space despite those constraints. Learned representations remain qualitatively similar and have similar training and generalization errors. They also agree across many measures with receptive fields measured in macaque V1. These findings support a more anatomically plausible model of compressed sparse coding, showing that the studied local wiring restrictions need not eliminate its representational benefits.
neurips-2020-learning-sparse-codes-from-.tldr: Structured random projections allow effective sparse coding under substantial local wiring constraints while retaining similarities to measured visual receptive fields.

paragraphs: In auctions where truthful bidding is not automatically optimal, a bidder's expected benefit depends on opponents' strategies and the distribution of their private information. Equilibria can therefore depend intricately on that distribution. This paper asks how many samples from it are sufficient to learn utilities and approximate equilibrium behavior.

Using first-price auctions as its main example, the paper shows that roughly n divided by epsilon squared samples, up to polylogarithmic factors, suffice to learn interim utilities for all monotone bidding strategies. Here n is the number of agents and epsilon is the accuracy parameter. The same sample count suffices to learn all approximate equilibria. An almost matching lower bound establishes that the utility-learning sample requirement is close to optimal.

The authors also study agents who must pay to discover their own private types. Through a connection to first-price auctions, they obtain the same sample scaling for estimating utilities and equilibria in a near-welfare-optimal descending auction. Along the way, they improve a sample-complexity bound for Pandora's Box, a model of sequential search.
neurips-2020-learning-utilities-and-equi.tldr: The paper establishes nearly tight sample requirements for learning utilities in first-price auctions and derives guarantees for approximate equilibria and costly-search settings.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains a policy entirely from previously collected data. Its central difficulty is distributional shift: the learned policy may visit situations poorly represented in that data. A learned dynamics model can support planning beyond recorded experiences, but its predictions may be unreliable where evidence is sparse.

MOPO addresses this problem by reducing rewards according to model uncertainty. The paper formulates offline model-based learning as optimization in a penalized Markov decision process and theoretically connects its objective to a lower bound on return in the true environment. The proposed algorithm uses the variance of a Lipschitz-regularized dynamics model as the reward penalty, making uncertain predictions less attractive during policy optimization.

The authors first observe that an existing model-based method already performs strongly offline, then report further gains from their uncertainty penalty. MOPO outperforms standard model-based methods and the compared leading model-free offline methods on the evaluated benchmarks. It also performs better on two continuous-control tasks requiring generalization from data gathered for a different task, supporting the usefulness of uncertainty-aware model-based learning beyond the original data-collection objective.
neurips-2020-mopo-model-based-offline-po.tldr: MOPO penalizes uncertain model predictions during offline reinforcement learning, improving tested policy performance and supporting generalization across tasks.

paragraphs: Children can use existing word knowledge to interpret a new word. If one object already has a label, they may assume the unfamiliar word refers to something else. This mutual exclusivity bias helps narrow down possible meanings without requiring repeated examples of every word-object pairing.

The paper investigates whether ordinary neural network architectures possess this learning bias. It finds that the examined vanilla architectures lack mutual exclusivity. This matters because success at learning associations from examples does not establish that a model will use known associations to resolve new ones in the same way. The study focuses attention on the assumptions built into learning, beyond the ability to fit observed mappings.

The authors also show that these architectures' inductive biases are poorly suited to lifelong formulations of classification and translation. Their contribution is a diagnosis and a research challenge: designing broadly applicable neural networks that learn through mutual exclusivity remains unresolved. The findings motivate making this learning assumption part of model design for settings in which new associations continue to arrive.
neurips-2020-mutual-exclusivity-as-a-cha.tldr: The studied vanilla neural networks lack mutual exclusivity, a useful human learning bias whose incorporation into general-purpose networks remains an open challenge.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows are generative models that support explicit probability-density calculation and efficient sample generation. Their transformations must be invertible, which constrains how each stage can represent data. Building expressive models through multiple such stages can therefore require a large number of parameters, making parameter efficiency an important scaling problem.

NanoFlow proposes using a single neural density estimator across multiple transformation stages. To make this shared estimator work, the paper introduces an efficient parameter decomposition and a flow indication embedding. The embedding supplies information about the transformation stage, allowing one neural network to participate in density estimation across the sequence rather than requiring fully separate estimators throughout.

Experiments on audio and image models support the resulting parameter efficiency. The authors report sublinear parameter complexity, meaning parameter requirements grow more slowly than a proportional increase as the flow scales in the studied scheme. The contribution is a way to parameterize larger flows more economically while retaining the density-estimation and synthesis capabilities that make this model family useful.
neurips-2020-nanoflow-scalable-normalizi.tldr: NanoFlow shares a neural density estimator across transformation stages to scale normalizing flows with sublinear parameter complexity.

paragraphs: Texture synthesis expands a small example into a larger image with a consistent pattern. The paper argues that conventional convolutional approaches struggle to generalize to unseen textures because their local operations are poorly matched to the global structure of this task. Repetition in textures motivates looking at the problem in the Fourier domain.

The authors interpret texture synthesis as local upsampling in that domain. Applying this idea directly to image Fourier transforms is difficult because their values span a large dynamic range and lack the local correlations useful to convolutional networks. The proposed framework therefore performs Fourier upsampling in feature space and uses deformable convolutions to make the construction suitable for learned synthesis.

The resulting model can synthesize textures from previously unseen images in a single pass. Extensive evaluations report state-of-the-art performance in both quantitative measurements and visual quality. The approach matters because it connects a global property of textures, their repetitive structure, to a representation where the synthesis operation can be learned effectively and reused across new examples.
neurips-2020-neural-ffts-for-universal-t.tldr: Fourier-domain upsampling in learned feature space enables single-pass texture synthesis that generalizes to unseen images.

paragraphs: Real Time Dynamic Programming plans online without requiring updates across the entire state space. This makes it useful when a problem has too many states to process together. The paper extends its usual one-step greedy decisions to an h-step lookahead policy, producing an algorithm called h-RTDP.

For the exact algorithm, the authors prove that longer lookahead improves sample complexity while requiring additional computation. Looking further ahead can therefore reduce the amount of sampled experience needed, at the expense of more planning work. The paper presents this as the first proof that increasing lookahead yields such a sample-complexity improvement in online planning.

The analysis also considers errors in the model, value updates, and state representation. In each approximate setting, h-RTDP has the same asymptotic performance as the corresponding approximate dynamic programming algorithm. Without further assumptions about approximation errors, the authors identify this as the strongest attainable comparison. The results clarify both the benefit of deeper planning and how its eventual performance relates to approximation quality.
neurips-2020-online-planning-with-lookah.tldr: Longer lookahead in h-RTDP provably improves sample complexity at additional computational cost and matches corresponding approximate dynamic programming asymptotically.

paragraphs: Distributed training can be slowed by communication between workers. Compression reduces the information sent, but decentralized methods must coordinate workers through a connected network without a central coordinator. Previous compressed approaches in this setting have required more complicated algorithms, extra memory, and additional hyperparameters.

This paper introduces an algorithm that directly compresses differences between neighboring workers' models using low-rank linear compressors. Inspired by PowerSGD, it applies power iteration to those differences to concentrate communication on informative components. The goal is to transfer more useful model information per bit while keeping the decentralized training procedure simple to use.

The authors prove faster convergence than prior methods without introducing additional hyperparameters. They also establish an asymptotic convergence behavior independent of the network and compression, a statement about the eventual regime rather than every stage of training. In deep learning benchmarks, the proposed compressors perform comparably to leading tuned compression algorithms without requiring that tuning. The findings combine a simpler algorithmic interface with theoretical and empirical support for effective communication compression.
neurips-2020-practical-low-rank-communic.tldr: Compressing neighboring workers' model differences with low-rank methods simplifies decentralized training and matches tuned compression methods in the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: A halfspace classifier separates points according to which side of a linear boundary they occupy. This paper studies learning such classifiers under differential privacy when the inputs lie on a finite grid in d-dimensional space. The aim is to reduce the number of training examples required while retaining the privacy guarantee.

The proposed learner has sample complexity approximately d to the power 2.5 times 2 raised to log-star of the grid size. Log-star denotes the number of repeated logarithms needed to reduce a quantity to a small constant. The result improves the prior state of the art by a factor of d squared, reducing the dimension-dependent sample requirement.

The key ingredient is a new private algorithm for approximate linear feasibility. Given a collection of linear inequalities that can all be satisfied, it privately constructs a point satisfying most of them. The algorithm determines one coordinate at each iteration. This coordinatewise construction supplies the building block for the improved learner, with the feasibility guarantee explicitly allowing some constraints to remain unsatisfied.
neurips-2020-private-learning-of-halfspa.tldr: A coordinatewise private feasibility algorithm reduces the sample complexity of learning halfspaces over finite grids by a factor of d squared.

paragraphs: A neural network's activation function determines the nonlinear transformations it can build between layers. This paper studies rational activations, which are ratios of polynomials. Their flexibility and smoothness make them an alternative to ReLU activations, and the authors investigate how that choice changes the complexity needed to approximate functions.

The main theoretical contribution establishes optimal bounds on network complexity. For approximating smooth functions, the authors prove that rational networks can be more efficient than ReLU networks, with exponentially smaller depth. This connects activation design directly to how many layers a representation requires, rather than treating the activation as a minor implementation choice.

Numerical experiments further demonstrate the appeal of rational activations. The theoretical result is specifically about approximation of smooth functions, so its significance lies in the representational advantage established for that setting. Together, the analysis and experiments make a case for exploring rational activations when smoothness and approximation efficiency matter, showing that changing the form of each nonlinearity can substantially affect the network architecture needed.
neurips-2020-rational-neural-networks-10.tldr: Rational activation functions enable provably more efficient approximation of smooth functions than ReLU networks, including exponentially smaller depth.

paragraphs: Self-imitation learning uses an agent's own previous experience to guide further learning, including when that experience came from a different policy. This paper generalizes the lower-bound Q-learning motivation for self-imitation by introducing an n-step lower bound. That extension produces a family of algorithms rather than a single return-based learning rule.

The theoretical analysis explains a possible source of improved performance through a trade-off between fixed-point bias and contraction rate. Fixed-point bias concerns the value estimate toward which learning settles; contraction rate concerns how quickly repeated updates approach that target. The analysis shows how n-step lower-bound learning balances these properties and relates it closely to uncorrected n-step Q-learning.

Across a broad range of benchmark tasks, the authors find the method more robust than return-based self-imitation and uncorrected n-step learning. The theory motivates potential gains rather than guaranteeing that every task improves. The empirical results support the practical value of the generalized bound, while the bias-and-contraction analysis gives a clearer account of why revisiting past experience can help.
neurips-2020-self-imitation-learning-via.tldr: An n-step lower bound generalizes self-imitation learning and offers a theoretically motivated trade-off that improves robustness in the evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: User-level differential privacy limits how much one person's data can change an algorithm's output distribution. When a person supplies many observations, those observations can improve estimation, but their larger influence may require more privacy noise. Choosing how much each person contributes is therefore part of the accuracy problem.

A simple approach caps the number of samples allowed from each user. This paper instead assigns weights to data points to bound contributions smoothly. Weighting provides a more gradual way to manage influence than a sample-count threshold. The authors apply the method to mean and quantile estimation, linear regression, and empirical risk minimization.

The paper proves that its algorithm outperforms the sample-limiting approach and reports experiments validating the theoretical results. The contribution is a different way to balance information use against the noise needed for privacy. By controlling contributions through appropriate weights, the method improves the stated utility trade-off across the estimation and learning problems considered, while continuing to treat the user as the unit whose influence must be protected.
neurips-2020-smoothly-bounding-user-cont.tldr: Smoothly weighting users' data improves the privacy–utility trade-off over limiting each user to a fixed number of samples.

paragraphs: Determining whether a connection is redundant in a recurrent network is difficult because information can travel through many interacting pathways. The paper proposes that neural noise could help reveal this structure. Correlations induced by noise may carry information about the wider network even when a learning rule observes only neighboring neurons.

The authors construct a local, unsupervised plasticity rule that either strengthens or removes a synapse. It uses only the synapse's weight and the noise-driven covariance of the neurons it connects. This offers a biologically plausible mechanism through which local measurements could guide pruning decisions that depend on broader patterns of connectivity.

For a subset of linear and rectified-linear networks, the authors prove that the rule preserves the original matrix's spectrum and consequently its network dynamics. The result holds even as the pruned fraction asymptotically approaches one. This is a guarantee for the specified network subset, while the biological interpretation remains a proposal: noise could serve a useful structural probing role in synaptic pruning.
neurips-2020-using-noise-to-probe-recurr.tldr: A local pruning rule uses noise-driven neural covariance and provably preserves dynamics under extensive pruning for a specified subset of networks.
